guidance: A field reader, not a validator, resolver or security check. It makes no DNS query and trusts the bytes you paste: a message that parses is not necessarily well formed for its purpose, and the decoder does not verify DNSSEC signatures, check zone consistency or decide whether a name is safe. Names are expanded through compression pointers only when a pointer refers to an earlier byte; a forward pointer is refused rather than followed, so a crafted message cannot loop the page. Types other than A, AAAA, CNAME, NS, PTR, MX, TXT, SOA, SRV, CAA and OPT are shown as raw hex because their structure is not interpreted, and UDP or TCP framing around the message is not part of the paste.
method: The message is read at the offsets RFC 1035 gives it: a 16-bit transaction ID, a 16-bit flags word (QR, opcode, AA, TC, RD, RA, Z, AD, CD and the 4-bit response code), four 16-bit counts, then the question and the answer, authority and additional records and their TTL, class and length-prefixed data. Names are read label by label; a length byte of 0xC0 is a pointer whose 14-bit offset must land earlier in the message, at most 64 pointers are followed, a label is at most 63 bytes and a whole name at most 255, so a forward pointer, a self pointer or an over-long name is refused with the byte offset rather than followed. A, AAAA, CNAME, NS, PTR, MX, TXT, SOA, SRV and CAA carry fixed or published layouts and are rendered field by field, AAAA in the RFC 5952 shortest form; the EDNS0 OPT pseudo-record (RFC 6891) reports its UDP payload size, extended response code, version and flags, and its options as code and length. Record lengths are checked against the bytes that remain, and an extended response code is combined with the header value. Type names come from the IANA DNS parameters registry, including the RFC 3597 TYPE form for unknown numbers. Everything runs in the browser with no uploads, storage or network calls.
